blog_post.body:
## What does freeze-dried instant coffee mean for an Indian kitchen?

Freeze-dried coffee skips the high-heat spray towers that strip aroma from most supermarket jars. Instead, the brew is frozen solid and the ice is lifted away under vacuum, so the volatile oils that carry chocolate, caramel, and fruit notes stay locked in the granule. For an Indian kitchen that means the cup you stir together at 6 a.m. still smells like the roastery, not like burnt toast. A practical tip: use water just off the boil — around 92 °C — and let the granules sit for ten seconds before stirring; the cooler splash protects the delicate top notes that boiling water would blow off. Purity Beans applies this method to Purica, the pure Arabica, and Purista, the pure Robusta, both at zero chicory. The 50 g jars are ₹329 and ₹319 respectively, and the 100 g jars are ₹559 and ₹509. When you pick up a jar of coffee off the grocery shelf, the ingredient list is usually where the marketing stops and reality begins. If you want true transparency, look for the exact coffee-to-chicory breakdown. Other jars in the lineup proudly feature pure coffee with zero chicory added, while some alternatives use entirely different processing methods like agglomeration instead of modern freeze-drying. By taking just five seconds to check that line before you buy, you immediately know whether you are pouring a rich, unblended brew or a chicory mix. It is a small habit that ensures your daily ritual matches your exact taste, keeping your kitchen stocked with precisely the kind of coffee you actually want to drink.
